entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10553"/><div sID="gen18825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10553"/>2. Inscription of the first prophecy.<div eID="gen18825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pharaoh-necho--</hi>He, when going against Carchemish (Cercusium, near the Euphrates), encountered Josiah, king of Judah (the ally of Assyria), at Megiddo, and slew him there (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.20-2Chr.35.24">2Ch 35:20-24</reference>); but he was four years subsequently overcome at Carchemish, by Nebuchadnezzar, as is foretold here; and lost all the territory which had been subject to the Pharaohs west of the Euphrates, and between it and the Nile. The prediction would mitigate the Jews' grief for Josiah, and show his death was not to be unavenged (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>). He is famed as having fitted out a fleet of discovery from the Red Sea, which doubled the Cape of Good Hope and returned to Egypt by the Mediterranean. <div eID="gen18826" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10558"/><div sID="gen18838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10558"/><hi type="bold">7. as a flood--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.47.2">Jr 47:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.22">Da 11:22</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10560"/><div sID="gen18841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10560"/>9. Ironical exhortation, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3">Jr 46:3</reference>. The Egyptians, owing to the heat of their climate and abstinence from animal food, were physically weak, and therefore employed mercenary soldiers.<div eID="gen18841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ethiopians--</hi>Hebrew, Cush: Abyssinia and Nubia.<div eID="gen18842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Libyans--</hi>Phut, Mauritania, west of Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Ge 10:6</reference>).<div eID="gen18843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shield--</hi>The Libyans borrowed from Egypt the use of the long shield extending to the feet [Xenophon, Cyropædia, 6 and 7].<div eID="gen18844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lydians--</hi>not the Lydians west of Asia Minor (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Ge 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>), but the Ludim, an African nation descended from Egypt (Mizraim) (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Ge 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.9">Na 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen18845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">handle and bend the bow--</hi>The employment of two verbs expresses the manner of bending the bow, namely, the foot being pressed on the center, and the hands holding the ends of it. <div eID="gen18846" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. Ironical exhortation, as in Jr 46:3 . The Egyptians, owing to the heat of their climate and abstinence from animal food, were physically weak, and therefore employed mercenary soldiers. Ethiopians-- Hebrew, Cush: Abyssinia and Nubia. Libyans-- Phut, Mauritania, west of Egypt (compare Ge 10:6 ). shield-- The Libyans borrowed from Egypt the use of the long shield extending to the feet [Xenophon, Cyropædia, 6 and 7]. Lydians-- not the Lydians west of Asia Minor ( Ge 10:22 ; Eze 30:5 ), but the Ludim, an African nation descended from Egypt (Mizraim) ( Ge 10:13 ; Eze 30:5 ; Na 3:9 ). handle and bend the bow-- The employment of two verbs expresses the manner of bending the bow, namely, the foot being pressed on the center, and the hands holding the ends of it.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10564"/><div sID="gen18854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10564"/>13-26. Prophecy of the invasion of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar, which took place sixteen years after the taking of Jerusalem. Having spent thirteen years in the siege of Tyre, and having obtained nothing for his pains, he is promised by God Egypt for his reward in humbling Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.20.30">Eze 29:17-20; 30</reference>:1-31:18). The intestine commotions between Amasis and Pharaoh-hophra prepared his way (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Is 19:1</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen18854" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10576"/><div sID="gen18885" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10576"/>27-28. Repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">Jr 30:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">11</reference>. When the Church (and literal Israel) might seem utterly consumed, there still remains hidden hope, because God, as it were, raises His people from the dead (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">Ro 11:15</reference>). Whereas the godless "nations" are consumed even though they survive, as are the Egyptians after their overthrow; because they are radically accursed and doomed [Calvin]. <chapter eID="Jer.46"/>
